message.content:
Prices across the semiconductor industry are moving upward in their cycle rather than easing, with memory costs rising and processor prices reported to be rising again [D3]. Those price pressures show up as demand-constrained cost pressures on compute and memory inputs rather than as excess supply [D7]. The value of shipments for computers and electronic products, the aggregate in which semiconductor shipments are included, has been rising, although those estimates are not adjusted for price changes [D1].

One thing driving prices is AI-related demand, which has made high-bandwidth memory a binding constraint as models scale and has left Korean export prices for semiconductors and DRAM as the accepted proxy for those input costs [D7]. A second driver is tightness in mature-node chips, where reported shortages are expected to persist and to turn supply chain management into a pricing lever [D3]. A third driver is the concentration of critical mineral processing and refining and of the specialised equipment ecosystem around a dominant supplier, which raises costs for diversified supply and has been aggravated by export controls extending to processing technologies and equipment [D4].

Working against further price increases is the expansion of semiconductor output, which is the indicator of supply growing to meet AI-driven demand and of continued cost relief in compute terms [D7]. Falling unit costs of compute, measured as the cost of leading GPUs per unit of memory bandwidth and per unit of compute, also push in the opposite direction to input prices [D7]. The pass-through of mineral costs to end products is weak because critical minerals account for a small share of downstream product prices [D4]. Order books point the same way as shipments, with new orders and unfilled orders for computers and electronic products rising, though those order series exclude semiconductor manufacturing itself [D6]. Domestic production of semiconductors and related electronic components has been expanding while the broader manufacturing operating rate remains below its long-run average, a configuration typical of a cycle in expansion rather than one that has peaked [D2]. The industry's growth outlook is expected to be strong, with geopolitical tension between the United States and China and the growth of the AI chip market identified as the forces that will shape it [D5].
